newsitem.title: USA: Man charged in Calif. shooting after McVeigh verdict.
newsitem.headline: Man charged in Calif. shooting after McVeigh verdict.

text.p: Federal prosecutors charged a former Army sharpshooter Friday with opening fire on a power substation -- apparently because he was upset by the Oklahoma City bombing verdict.
Peter Brooks Jaffe, a U.S. Army veteran and weapons expert who is homeless, faces federal destruction of property and weapons charges, according to the criminal complaint.
No one was injured in Tuesday's early morning attack, but the bullets knocked out power to homes near the Emerald Lake substation, owned by PG&E Corp 's Pacific Gas and Electric Co.

At his arraignment in San Francisco Friday, Jaffe, 42, did not enter a plea. Redwood City police said Jaffe, who was arrested Wednesday, confessed to the shooting and told investigators that he was angry at the way the government treated him and other veterans.

Police and the FBI said they believed the shooting was prompted by Monday's conviction in Denver of Timothy McVeigh, a Gulf War veteran, for setting off the truck bomb that destroyed the federal building in Oklahoma City in April 1995, killing 168 people.
Investigators found more than 55 rifle shell casings around the PG&E substation, a newspaper bearing the headline "McVeigh Guilty," and a Confederate flag on a nearby fence.
"He felt that McVeigh was also a victim of a government cover up," said Redwood City Police Detective Donald Banks. "He mentioned to a girlfriend he was going to avenge McVeigh."
Jaffe used a military-style assault rifle in the substation attack, a weapon similar to the M-16 rifle Jaffe used as an Army sharpshooter in the late 1970s, police said.
Police said Jaffe told investigators he targeted PG&E because he believed the company worked closely with the government and because the attack would get media attention.

The shooting knocked out power to about 2,000 Pacific Gas and Electric customers. Two transformers at the substation were taken out of service because of the damage, estimated at $500,000, a company spokeswoman said.
If convicted, Jaffe faces up to 15 years in prison and fines of $250,000 on each count.
